senses.gloss: So simple or well designed that it cannot go wrong or be used wrongly.
examples: There's no *foolproof* way to pick the right stock.
The instructions are so clear they're practically *foolproof*.
She has a *foolproof* recipe for chocolate chip cookies.

position: both — most often after a verb or in *footloose and fancy-free*

senses.gloss: Free to go where you like and do what you want, with no responsibilities.
examples: After college he spent a *footloose* year traveling through Asia.
She's single and *footloose* and can move anywhere for work.
They were young, *footloose* and fancy-free.

contrast: Not the same as *forbidding*, which means unfriendly or threatening-looking: *a forbidden room* is one you may not enter; *a forbidding room* looks cold and unwelcoming.

senses.gloss: Not allowed by a rule, a law or custom.
examples: Smoking is *forbidden* anywhere on campus.
As kids we were fascinated by the *forbidden* room in the basement.
Money was a *forbidden* topic at our dinner table.

contrast: Not the same as *forbidden* (not allowed): *a forbidding place* looks unfriendly or dangerous; *a forbidden place* is one you may not enter.

senses.gloss: Looking unfriendly, threatening or difficult, so that you do not want to go near.
examples: The old prison was a gray, *forbidding* building.
The mountains looked even more *forbidding* in the fog.
His boss had a *forbidding* expression that kept people from asking questions.

comparison: not gradable — the 'unnatural' sense takes *more/most*: *more forced*

senses.gloss: Done because you have to or are made to, not because you choose.
examples: The plane made a *forced* landing in a cornfield.
Millions of people were sent to *forced* labor camps.
The company announced a round of *forced* retirements.

senses.gloss: Not sincere or natural; done with obvious effort.
examples: She gave a *forced* smile and said she was fine.
The jokes in the script felt *forced*.
His cheerfulness seemed even more *forced* after the news.

contrast: *forceful* is about a strong, confident manner: *a forceful argument*. *forcible* is about physical force: *forcible entry*.

senses.gloss: Strong and confident in expressing opinions or taking action.
examples: She's a *forceful* speaker who holds the room.
The mayor made a *forceful* case for the new tax.
He needs to be more *forceful* in meetings.

contrast: *forcible* means using physical force; *forceful* means strong and confident: *a forceful speaker*.

senses.gloss: Done by using physical force.
examples: Police found no signs of *forcible* entry.
The court ruled against the *forcible* removal of the protesters.
They opposed the *forcible* relocation of families from the area.

contrast: More often a noun: *a sense of foreboding*, *full of foreboding*.

senses.gloss: Making you feel that something bad is going to happen.
examples: *Foreboding* clouds gathered over the lake.
The music grew dark and *foreboding*.
The empty house looked even more *foreboding* at night.

position: attributive only — or as a noun: *the foregoing*
contrast: Formal writing only. Do not confuse with *forgoing*, from *forgo* (to give something up).

senses.gloss: Just mentioned, or coming before this in a text; used in formal writing.
examples: The *foregoing* discussion shows the limits of the study.
In light of the *foregoing* facts, the motion is denied.
All of the *foregoing* examples come from court records.

position: attributive only — almost always in *a foregone conclusion*

senses.gloss: Certain even before it happens, so there is no real doubt about it.
examples: The outcome of the election was a *foregone* conclusion.
Don't treat a win as a *foregone* conclusion — we still have to play.
Most fans saw the trade as a *foregone* conclusion.

position: both — the 'other countries' and 'foreign object' senses only before a noun
comparison: not gradable — the 'unfamiliar' sense takes *more/most*: *more foreign*
contrast: Use *foreign* for things: *foreign cars*, *foreign languages*. For people, *foreigner* can sound unfriendly; Americans often say *international students* or *visitors from abroad* instead.

senses.gloss: From, in or typical of a country that is not your own.
examples: She speaks three *foreign* languages.
Most of the cars in the lot were *foreign*.
The city attracts millions of *foreign* tourists every year.

senses.gloss: Dealing with or involving other countries.
examples: The president's *foreign* policy was unpopular.
She reports on *foreign* affairs for a Chicago paper.

senses.gloss: Strange and unfamiliar to someone.
examples: The idea of saving money was completely *foreign* to him.
Life on a farm felt *foreign* at first.

senses.gloss: Coming from outside and not belonging where it is found.
examples: The X-ray showed a *foreign* object in his stomach.
The doctor removed a *foreign* body from the child's ear.

senses.gloss: Born in another country and now living in this one.
examples: About a third of the city's residents are *foreign-born*.
The study tracked *foreign-born* workers in the tech industry.
Her *foreign-born* parents never lost their accents.

comparison: not gradable — it already means 'most important'
contrast: *first and foremost* is an adverb phrase meaning 'most importantly': *First and foremost, we need a plan.*

senses.gloss: Most important, or best known in a particular field.
examples: She is one of the country's *foremost* experts on climate.
Safety should be *foremost* in everyone's mind.
The museum holds the region's *foremost* collection of Native American art.

senses.gloss: Using scientific methods to investigate crimes or to provide evidence in court.
examples: The *forensic* team collected fingerprints from the door.
*Forensic* evidence linked him to the scene.
She works as a *forensic* accountant for the FBI.

senses.gloss: Possible to know about or expect in advance.
examples: The accident was entirely *foreseeable*.
The bridge collapse was a *foreseeable* result of years of neglect.

senses.gloss: In *the foreseeable future*: for as far ahead as anyone can reasonably plan.
examples: We don't plan to hire anyone for the *foreseeable* future.
Prices will stay high in the *foreseeable* future.

senses.gloss: Covered with trees.
examples: The trail winds through *forested* hills.
Much of northern Maine is heavily *forested*.
They bought ten acres of *forested* land.

senses.gloss: Copied illegally so that it looks real.
examples: He was arrested for using a *forged* passport.
The signature on the check was *forged*.
Police found boxes of *forged* documents.

senses.gloss: Shaped by heating metal and hammering it.
examples: The gate is made of *forged* iron.
These knives are *forged*, not stamped.

senses.gloss: Often forgetting things.
examples: My grandmother is getting more *forgetful*.
I'm so *forgetful* — I left my keys in the door again.
Stress and lack of sleep can make you *forgetful*.

senses.gloss: Not interesting or special enough to remember.
examples: The movie was entertaining but *forgettable*.
He had a *forgettable* season after his injury.
It was one of the most *forgettable* meals I've ever eaten.

senses.gloss: Not so bad that it cannot be forgiven.
examples: Being late once is *forgivable*; being late every day isn't.
It was an easy, *forgivable* mistake.
Lying to protect a friend seemed more *forgivable* to her.

senses.gloss: Willing to forgive people for what they have done wrong.
examples: My mom was always more *forgiving* than my dad.
Voters are not always *forgiving* of scandals.

senses.gloss: Allowing for mistakes or rough use without causing problems.
examples: This racket is very *forgiving* for beginners.
Stretchy fabric is *forgiving* if you gain a few pounds.

senses.gloss: No longer remembered, noticed or cared about.
examples: We found a *forgotten* box of letters in the attic.
The small towns along the old highway feel *forgotten*.
By the 1980s the singer was largely *forgotten*.

senses.gloss: Divided into two or more parts at one end.
examples: Snakes have *forked* tongues.
A *forked* branch makes a good slingshot.
*Forked* lightning lit up the sky.

position: both — the 'hopeless' sense only before a noun

senses.gloss: Sad and lonely, or looking empty and abandoned.
examples: A *forlorn* puppy sat alone in the rain.
The empty mall looked *forlorn*.
She looked more *forlorn* than ever.

senses.gloss: Very unlikely to succeed.
examples: They made a *forlorn* attempt to save the factory.
Peace now seems a *forlorn* hope.

position: both — the 'official' and 'education' senses usually before a noun
contrast: False friend. Russian *формальный подход* (done only for show) is *perfunctory* or *box-ticking* in English, not *formal*. English *formal* means serious and official in style.

senses.gloss: Serious and correct in style, following the rules for official occasions, clothes or language.
examples: The wedding invitation says *formal* attire.
Use *formal* language in a cover letter.
He's more *formal* than his brother and always calls me Ms. Chen.

senses.gloss: Official and done according to the proper rules.
examples: She filed a *formal* complaint with HR.
We haven't received a *formal* offer yet.
There was no *formal* agreement between them.

senses.gloss: Received through schools, colleges and training programs.
senses.ru: систематическое, полученное в учебном заведении (об образовании)
examples: He had little *formal* education but read constantly.
She has no *formal* training in design.

senses.gloss: Made official, or given a fixed structure and rules.
examples: The company has no *formalized* process for hiring.
The rules became more *formalized* as the club grew.
Most schools now have *formalized* anti-bullying policies.

senses.gloss: Having a strong influence on how a person or thing develops.
examples: She spent her *formative* years in Detroit.
Losing his father was the most *formative* experience of his life.
Teaching abroad was *formative* for me.

senses.gloss: Impressive and powerful, and a little frightening.
examples: She was a *formidable* opponent in debate.
The team looks even more *formidable* this year.
He has a *formidable* memory for names.

senses.gloss: Very difficult to deal with.
examples: Rebuilding the town is a *formidable* task.
The mountain presents *formidable* challenges for climbers.

senses.gloss: Following a fixed pattern and lacking originality.
examples: Most romantic comedies are pretty *formulaic*.
The speech was full of *formulaic* phrases.
Her later novels became more *formulaic*.

position: both — the 'coming soon' sense before a noun, the other two after a verb
comparison: not gradable — the 'willing to talk' sense takes *more/most*: *more forthcoming*
contrast: The meaning changes with position: *a forthcoming report* will appear soon; *he wasn't forthcoming* means he didn't say much; *no help was forthcoming* means none was given.

senses.gloss: Going to happen or appear soon.
examples: Her *forthcoming* book is about the Civil War.
Details will be announced in a *forthcoming* report.

senses.gloss: Willing to give information or talk openly.
examples: He wasn't very *forthcoming* about his past.
The company has been more *forthcoming* since the lawsuit.

senses.gloss: Given or provided when needed; usually in negative sentences.
examples: No explanation was *forthcoming*.
If funding isn't *forthcoming*, the project will stop.

senses.gloss: Saying honestly and directly what you think.
examples: She's *forthright* about her political views.
He gave a *forthright* answer to a tough question.
I wish my manager were more *forthright* with us.

takes: *with* + noun, in the 'with something added' sense

senses.gloss: Protected by walls or other defenses against attack.
examples: The soldiers held a *fortified* position on the hill.
The old city is *fortified* with thick stone walls.

senses.gloss: Having something added to make it healthier or stronger.
examples: Most breakfast cereals are *fortified* with iron.
Port is a *fortified* wine.
Buy milk that is *fortified* with vitamin D.

contrast: Strictly it means 'by chance', but most Americans now use it to mean 'lucky' as well, and the two meanings usually overlap.

senses.gloss: Happening by chance, especially by a lucky chance.
examples: Our meeting at the airport was completely *fortuitous*.
A *fortuitous* phone call led to her first job.
The timing could not have been more *fortuitous*.

senses.gloss: Lucky, or having good things that other people do not have.
examples: We were *fortunate* to find an apartment so quickly.
It's *fortunate* that nobody was hurt.
We should help people who are less *fortunate* than we are.

position: both — the direction and front senses before a noun, the 'too bold' sense after a verb
comparison: not gradable — the 'too bold' sense takes *more/most*: *more forward*
contrast: Usually an adverb: *step forward*, *look forward to*. The adjective is the one before a noun (*forward motion*) or the 'too bold' sense (*a bit forward*).

senses.gloss: Moving or directed toward the front or ahead.
examples: The team made little *forward* progress in the second half.
Lean your body into a slightly *forward* position.
A *forward* pass is legal in football but not in rugby.

senses.gloss: At or near the front of a ship, plane or vehicle.
examples: Passengers in the *forward* cabin get off first.
The *forward* seats have more legroom.

senses.gloss: Too confident or friendly with someone you do not know well.
examples: It was a little *forward* of him to ask for her number so soon.
I hope I'm not being too *forward*.
She was more *forward* than the other girls in class.

senses.gloss: Planning for the future and open to new ideas.
examples: The city has a *forward-looking* plan for public transit.
She's one of the most *forward-looking* leaders in the industry.
The report contains *forward-looking* statements about profits.

comparison: not gradable — the 'unable to change' sense takes *more/most*: *more fossilized*

senses.gloss: Turned into a fossil.
examples: They found *fossilized* dinosaur bones in Montana.
The rock contains *fossilized* shells.

senses.gloss: Fixed and unable to change or develop.
examples: The party is run by a *fossilized* leadership.
His ideas about women seem *fossilized*.
Teachers call mistakes that never go away *fossilized* errors.

contrast: *foster* parents care for a child for a time; *adoptive* parents become the child's legal parents for good. Russian *приёмный* covers both. *to foster* is also a verb: *foster a child*, *foster cooperation*.

senses.gloss: Caring for a child in a family for a period of time without becoming the legal parents, or being cared for in this way.
examples: They've been *foster* parents to more than twenty kids.
She grew up in a series of *foster* homes.
The shelter is looking for *foster* families for puppies.

contrast: Also a noun and a verb in sports: *commit a foul*, *he fouled out*. Sounds the same as *fowl* (birds such as chickens).

senses.gloss: Very unpleasant to smell or taste.
examples: A *foul* smell was coming from the fridge.
The water tasted *foul*.
It was the *foulest* coffee I've ever had.

senses.gloss: Very bad or unpleasant, of weather, a mood or a temper.
examples: He's been in a *foul* mood all day.
*Foul* weather delayed the launch.

senses.gloss: Rude and offensive, full of swearing.
examples: The coach was fined for *foul* language.
She has a *foul* mouth when she's angry.

senses.gloss: Against the rules or the law; in baseball, hit outside the lines.
examples: The umpire called it a *foul* ball.
Police suspect *foul* play in his death.

senses.gloss: Using a lot of rude, offensive words.
examples: The comedian is famous for his *foul-mouthed* rants.
My uncle gets *foul-mouthed* when he watches football.
She was the most *foul-mouthed* kid in the neighborhood.

senses.gloss: Having a very unpleasant smell.
examples: A *foul-smelling* liquid leaked from the truck.
The river became *foul-smelling* in the summer heat.
The swamp was the most *foul-smelling* place on the trip.

contrast: *four-wheel drive* (4WD) is the system; a car that has it is *a four-wheel-drive vehicle*, or informally *a four-by-four*.

senses.gloss: Having four wheels, or with the engine's power sent to all four wheels.
examples: You'll need *four-wheel* drive on those mountain roads.
Kids rode *four-wheel* ATVs across the field.
*Four-wheel* vehicles aren't allowed on the beach.

contrast: Also an adverb: *Prices rose fourfold.*

senses.gloss: Four times as big or as many; or having four parts.
examples: There has been a *fourfold* increase in cases since May.
The company saw a *fourfold* rise in profits.
The program has a *fourfold* purpose.

senses.gloss: Informal and a little dated: sexually attractive, usually of a woman.
examples: He thinks his new neighbor is pretty *foxy*.
She looked *foxy* in that leather jacket.

senses.gloss: Clever and good at tricking people.
examples: He's the *foxiest* negotiator I know.
The *foxy* old senator knew exactly how to get votes.

senses.gloss: Very small.
examples: Stocks rose by a *fractional* amount.
The new model is only a *fractional* improvement.

senses.gloss: Relating to fractions, or to parts of a whole.
examples: *Fractional* numbers confuse a lot of kids.
They bought *fractional* ownership of a vacation home.

senses.gloss: Easily annoyed and hard to control, or always arguing.
examples: The *fractious* toddler refused to take a nap.
The party is deeply divided and *fractious*.
Negotiations grew more *fractious* as the deadline neared.

contrast: American *fragile* rhymes with *agile*: FRAJ-uhl, not the British FRAJ-yl.

senses.gloss: Easily broken or damaged.
examples: Be careful — those glasses are *fragile*.
Old books have *fragile* pages.

senses.gloss: Weak and easily made worse or destroyed, of peace, health or an economy.
examples: The ceasefire remains *fragile*.
The economy is more *fragile* than it looks.

senses.gloss: Emotionally weak and easily upset.
examples: She's still feeling *fragile* after the breakup.
He has a *fragile* ego.

senses.gloss: Made of small separate parts and incomplete.
examples: We only have *fragmentary* evidence of what happened.
Early reports from the scene were *fragmentary*.
The historical record is even more *fragmentary* for that period.

senses.gloss: Broken into separate parts that do not fit or work well together.
examples: The health care system is badly *fragmented*.
Social media has created a more *fragmented* audience.
I only have *fragmented* memories of that night.

senses.gloss: Having a pleasant smell.
examples: The garden was full of *fragrant* roses.
The kitchen smelled warm and *fragrant* with cinnamon.
Jasmine is more *fragrant* at night.

senses.gloss: Physically weak and thin, usually because of old age or illness.
examples: My grandfather has grown *frail* since his surgery.
A *frail* old woman answered the door.
She looked *frailer* than I remembered.

senses.gloss: Easily damaged or broken; not strong.
examples: The *frail* wooden bridge swayed in the wind.
The country's *frail* economy could not survive another shock.

contrast: *to be framed* can also mean to be made to look guilty of a crime — that is the verb *frame*, not this adjective.

senses.gloss: Put in a frame.
examples: A *framed* photo of her parents hung by the door.
Is the print *framed*, or is it just a poster?
He keeps his diploma *framed* on the office wall.

senses.gloss: Honest and direct, even when the truth is unpleasant.
examples: Let me be *frank* — your work hasn't been good enough.
We had a *frank* discussion about money.
The doctor was *franker* with me than I expected.

senses.gloss: So worried or afraid that you cannot control your feelings.
examples: Her parents were *frantic* when she didn't come home.
He made a *frantic* call to 911.

senses.gloss: Done very fast and in a hurried, disorganized way.
examples: There was a *frantic* search for the missing ring.
Things get more *frantic* at the restaurant around eight.

senses.gloss: Of or like brothers; friendly and supportive, or relating to a club of members who help each other.
examples: The two leaders spoke of *fraternal* ties between their countries.
He felt a *fraternal* bond with his teammates.
The Elks is a *fraternal* organization.

senses.gloss: Of twins, developed from two separate eggs and so not identical.
examples: My sister and I are *fraternal* twins.
*Fraternal* twins can be a boy and a girl.

senses.gloss: Intended to cheat people, often illegally.
examples: The bank flagged several *fraudulent* charges on my card.
His insurance claim turned out to be *fraudulent*.
They were sued for *fraudulent* advertising.

position: both — *fraught with* only after a verb

senses.gloss: Full of something bad, such as danger or problems.
examples: The journey was *fraught* with danger.
Buying a used car can be *fraught* with problems.

senses.gloss: Causing or feeling a lot of worry and tension.
examples: She has a *fraught* relationship with her father.
The mood in the office was more *fraught* than usual.

senses.gloss: Worn at the edges, so that loose threads show.
examples: His jeans were *frayed* at the cuffs.
Replace that *frayed* cord before it starts a fire.

senses.gloss: Strained and close to breaking, of nerves, tempers or relationships.
examples: Tempers were *frayed* after hours in traffic.
Our nerves were *frayed* by the time the results came in.

senses.gloss: Very unusual and strange, often in a way that seems unnatural.
examples: A *freakish* storm dropped snow in May.
He has *freakish* strength for his size.
It was a *freakish* accident that nobody could have predicted.

senses.gloss: Informal: strange and a little frightening.
examples: That movie was really *freaky*.
It's *freaky* how much you look like your mom.
That's the *freakiest* thing that's ever happened to me.

senses.gloss: Covered with freckles, small brown spots on the skin.
examples: A *freckled* boy with red hair waved at us.
Her arms were *freckled* from the sun.
He had a *freckled* nose and a big smile.

senses.gloss: Of farm animals, or their eggs or meat: allowed to move around outside rather than kept in cages.
examples: We only buy *free-range* eggs.
The chickens on this farm are *free-range*.
*Free-range* turkey costs more at Thanksgiving.

senses.gloss: Informal: of children, allowed to play and go places without constant adult supervision.
examples: They believe in *free-range* parenting.
We had a *free-range* childhood, biking all over town.

contrast: Also an adverb: *She drew the map freehand.*

senses.gloss: Drawn by hand without a ruler, stencil or other tool.
examples: He made a quick *freehand* sketch of the building.
The artist is known for her *freehand* lettering.
The tattoo was a *freehand* design.

contrast: Also an adverb and a verb: *work freelance*, *she freelances*. The person is a *freelancer*.

senses.gloss: Working for different companies and paid for each job, rather than employed by one company.
examples: She's a *freelance* graphic designer.
Most of the writers at the magazine are *freelance*.
He does *freelance* work on weekends.

senses.gloss: Standing on its own, not attached to a wall or another building.
examples: We replaced the built-in tub with a *freestanding* one.
The garage is *freestanding*, not attached to the house.
Many of the town's *freestanding* stores have closed.

senses.gloss: Not worried about rules or responsibilities; free and informal.
examples: The show is known for its *freewheeling* interviews.
He lived a *freewheeling* life in 1970s California.
The early days of the internet were far more *freewheeling*.

senses.gloss: Preserved by freezing it quickly and then removing the water.
examples: Astronauts eat *freeze-dried* food.
We packed *freeze-dried* meals for the camping trip.
Most instant coffee is *freeze-dried*.

senses.gloss: Fast, energetic and uncontrolled.
examples: New York has a *frenetic* pace of life.
The band played a *frenetic* set.
The last week before launch was even more *frenetic*.

senses.gloss: Wild, excited and out of control.
examples: The sale set off *frenzied* shopping at the mall.
Sharks began a *frenzied* attack on the bait.
The crowd grew more *frenzied* as the band came on stage.

contrast: The adjective is stressed on the first syllable, FREE-kwuhnt. The formal verb *to frequent* (to go somewhere often) is often stressed on the second: free-KWENT.

senses.gloss: Happening or doing something often.
examples: She's a *frequent* flyer on Delta.
Power outages are *frequent* here in winter.
Storms have become more *frequent* in recent years.

position: both — the 'just come from' and 'rude' senses after a verb
takes: *from* or *out of* + noun, in the 'just come from' sense

senses.gloss: Recently made, picked or caught; not old, frozen or canned.
examples: We bought *fresh* corn at the farmers market.
Is this bread *fresh*?
The *freshest* fish comes in on Tuesday mornings.

senses.gloss: New or different, replacing something old or used.
examples: After the divorce she wanted a *fresh* start.
The team needs some *fresh* ideas.
Let me get you a *fresh* towel.

senses.gloss: Recent, just done, or still clear in the mind.
examples: The memory is still *fresh* in my mind.
Watch out for the *fresh* paint!
There was a foot of *fresh* snow on the ground.

senses.gloss: Of air or a smell: clean, cool and pleasant.
examples: Let's go outside and get some *fresh* air.
The sheets had a *fresh*, clean smell.

senses.gloss: Of water: not salty.
examples: The island has no source of *fresh* water.
These fish can't survive in *fresh* water.

senses.gloss: Full of energy; not tired.
examples: I felt *fresh* after a good night's sleep.
She looked *fresher* after a shower and a coffee.

senses.gloss: Having just come from a place, school or experience.
examples: He's *fresh* out of college.
The chef came to us *fresh* from a job in Paris.

senses.gloss: Informal and a little old-fashioned: rude or disrespectful, often in a sexual way.
examples: Don't get *fresh* with me, young man.
He got *fresh* with the waitress and was asked to leave.

senses.gloss: Worried and unable to relax; of a baby, crying and restless.
examples: The baby was *fretful* all night with a fever.
She spent a *fretful* week waiting for the test results.
He grew more *fretful* as the flight was delayed again.

senses.gloss: Relating to Sigmund Freud and his theories of the mind.
examples: The novel is full of *Freudian* symbols.
Her therapist takes a *Freudian* approach.

senses.gloss: Showing hidden, often sexual, thoughts or feelings — especially in *a Freudian slip*.
examples: Calling my boss 'Mom' was a *Freudian* slip.
There's something very *Freudian* about his fear of snakes.

senses.gloss: In physics, having no friction.
examples: Imagine a ball rolling on a *frictionless* surface.
No real machine is completely *frictionless*.

senses.gloss: Smooth and easy, with no delays or difficulties.
examples: The app promises *frictionless* payments.
Online shopping has become almost *frictionless*.
The company wants a more *frictionless* checkout.

position: both — the informal senses after a verb
contrast: *fried* means cooked in oil or fat. Russian *жареный* also covers roasting and grilling: meat cooked in the oven is *roast*, on a grill *grilled*. Food cooked covered in hot oil is *deep-fried*.

senses.gloss: Cooked in hot oil or fat.
examples: She ordered *fried* chicken and mashed potatoes.
Do you want your eggs *fried* or scrambled?
Too much *fried* food is bad for your heart.

senses.gloss: Informal: very tired and unable to think clearly.
examples: My brain is *fried* after that exam.
I'm totally *fried* — I need a break.

senses.gloss: Informal: of electronics, destroyed by too much electricity or heat.
examples: The storm left our router *fried*.
Check whether the motherboard is *fried*.

contrast: A little old-fashioned; everyday American English says *terrible* or *awful*. It is not the same as *frightening* (causing fear).

senses.gloss: Very bad, unpleasant or shocking.
examples: The traffic downtown was *frightful*.
Survivors described the *frightful* conditions in the camp.
Oh, the weather outside is *frightful*.

contrast: False friend. Russian *фригидный* is only about sex; that sense of *frigid* is old-fashioned and offensive in English. Americans most often use *frigid* about weather and water.

senses.gloss: Very cold.
examples: *Frigid* air moved into the Midwest overnight.
The water in the lake was *frigid*.
It was the most *frigid* January on record.

senses.gloss: Unfriendly and without any warmth.
examples: She gave him a *frigid* stare.
The meeting ended on a *frigid* note.

senses.gloss: Decorated with a lot of frills, wavy strips of cloth or lace.
examples: The little girl wore a pink *frilly* dress.
Her bedroom was full of *frilly* pillows.
This year's wedding dresses are *frillier* than ever.

senses.gloss: Full of energy and wanting to play.
examples: The puppy gets *frisky* in the morning.
The horses were *friskier* in the cold weather.

senses.gloss: Informal: feeling playful in a sexual way.
examples: After a couple of drinks, he got a little *frisky*.
The couple got *frisky* on the dance floor.

senses.gloss: Not serious or sensible about things that matter.
examples: She was tired of his *frivolous* attitude toward work.
Don't be so *frivolous* — this is a serious decision.

senses.gloss: Having no real purpose or value.
examples: The judge threw out the *frivolous* lawsuit.
He spends too much on *frivolous* purchases.
Critics called the new spending even more *frivolous*.

senses.gloss: Of hair: tightly curled and dry, often in a messy way.
examples: Humidity makes my hair *frizzy*.
She had big *frizzy* hair in the eighties.
My hair gets *frizzier* every summer.

contrast: *in front of* is a preposition: *in front of the house* means outside, facing it; *at the front of the house* means in its forward part.

senses.gloss: At or near the front part of something.
examples: Please use the *front* door.
We got seats in the *front* row.
He lost two *front* teeth in a fight.

senses.gloss: Aimed directly at the front; direct and open.
examples: The army launched a *frontal* assault on the city.
Her speech was a *frontal* attack on the president's policies.

senses.gloss: Relating to the front of the head or brain.
examples: Damage to the *frontal* lobe can change a person's behavior.
The *frontal* bone forms the forehead.

senses.gloss: Damaged by extreme cold.
examples: The climbers returned with *frostbitten* toes.
His fingers were badly *frostbitten*.
The *frostbitten* plants turned black overnight.

contrast: American *frosting* is British *icing*, so *a frosted cake* is a cake covered with icing.

senses.gloss: Of glass: made rough so that you cannot see through it clearly.
examples: The bathroom window has *frosted* glass.
She knocked on a *frosted* glass door marked 'Private.'

senses.gloss: Covered with frosting, a sweet creamy topping, or with sugar.
examples: The kids ate *frosted* cupcakes at the party.
He only likes *frosted* cereal.

senses.gloss: Covered with frost.
examples: The *frosted* grass crunched under our boots.
The car windows were *frosted* over.

senses.gloss: Very cold, with frost on the ground or on surfaces.
examples: It was a *frosty* morning in November.
The nights are getting *frostier*.
He grabbed a *frosty* bottle of beer from the cooler.

senses.gloss: Unfriendly and cold in manner.
examples: She gave me a *frosty* look.
Relations between the two neighbors are *frosty*.

senses.gloss: Full of or covered with small bubbles.
examples: She ordered a *frothy* cappuccino.
Beat the eggs until they're *frothy*.

senses.gloss: Light, fun and not serious.
examples: It's a *frothy* summer comedy.
Her new novel is even *frothier* than the last one.

senses.gloss: Of a market or prices: rising too fast and likely to fall.
examples: Analysts warned that the housing market was *frothy*.
Tech stocks look *frothy* right now.

senses.gloss: Turned into ice, or made hard by cold.
examples: The kids went skating on the *frozen* pond.
The ground was *frozen* solid.

senses.gloss: Of food: kept at a very low temperature to preserve it.
examples: Grab a bag of *frozen* peas.
*Frozen* pizza is his idea of dinner.
Is the chicken fresh or *frozen*?

senses.gloss: Of a person: very cold.
examples: Come inside — you must be *frozen*!
My feet are *frozen*.

senses.gloss: Unable to move because of fear or shock.
examples: She stood *frozen* in the doorway.
He was *frozen* with fear.

senses.gloss: Of money, prices or a screen: fixed and not able to change or move.
examples: Their bank accounts are still *frozen*.
My screen is *frozen* again.

contrast: Of a person, *frugal* and *thrifty* are praise and *cheap* or *stingy* are criticism. *economical* is usually about things: *an economical car*.

senses.gloss: Careful to spend very little money.
examples: My parents were *frugal* and never bought anything on credit.
We'll need to be more *frugal* this year.
He's *frugal*, but he's not cheap.

senses.gloss: Of a meal: simple and cheap.
examples: They ate a *frugal* dinner of beans and rice.
The monks lived on *frugal* meals.

senses.gloss: Producing good or useful results.
examples: We had a *fruitful* meeting with the investors.
The partnership has been *fruitful* for both companies.
This year's talks were more *fruitful* than last year's.

senses.gloss: Producing no useful result.
examples: After a *fruitless* search, they called the police.
Our efforts to reach him were *fruitless*.
She spent years on a *fruitless* attempt to get the case reopened.

contrast: *fruity* means tasting or smelling of fruit. Something made from fruit uses the noun *fruit* before the noun: *fruit juice*, *fruit salad*, not *fruity juice*.

senses.gloss: Tasting or smelling of fruit.
examples: This wine is light and *fruity*.
The candle has a sweet, *fruity* smell.
The red is *fruitier* than the white.

senses.gloss: Wearing plain, old-fashioned clothes that make a person, usually a woman, look unattractive; of clothes, making someone look this way.
examples: She felt *frumpy* next to her stylish friends.
I don't want a *frumpy* sweater — show me something more modern.
That dress makes me look *frumpier* than my grandmother.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun, usually two words after a verb: *it's fucked up*
form: compound — participle + particle, from the phrasal verb *fuck up*
contrast: Vulgar slang and highly offensive — avoid it at work and with people you don't know. The polite version is *messed-up*.

senses.gloss: Vulgar slang: very bad, wrong, unfair or badly damaged.
examples: That's a *fucked-up* thing to say to your sister.
The whole situation is *fucked up*.

senses.gloss: Vulgar slang: mentally or emotionally damaged.
examples: He was pretty *fucked up* after the war.
She had a *fucked-up* childhood.

senses.gloss: Vulgar slang: very drunk or high on drugs.
examples: Everyone at the party was completely *fucked up*.
He got *fucked up* on cheap vodka.

contrast: Vulgar and highly offensive. Before an adjective or adverb it is an adverb (*fucking cold*), not this adjective. Milder: *freaking*, *damn*.

senses.gloss: Vulgar slang: used before a noun to add strong emphasis, anger or annoyance.
examples: Where are my *fucking* keys?
This whole meeting is a *fucking* joke.
Turn off that *fucking* music!

contrast: American spelling is *fulfill*, *fulfilled*, *fulfillment*; British spelling drops an *l*: *fulfil*, *fulfilment*.

senses.gloss: Happy and satisfied because you are doing something useful or using your abilities fully.
examples: She feels *fulfilled* in her work as a nurse.
He wanted a more *fulfilled* life than his father had.
Retirement left him bored and far from *fulfilled*.

comparison: not gradable — the 'wholehearted' sense takes *more/most*: *more full-blooded*

senses.gloss: Of pure ancestry, with both parents from the same group or breed.
examples: The breeder sells *full-blooded* Arabian horses.
My grandfather was a *full-blooded* Italian and cooked like one.

senses.gloss: Strong, enthusiastic and complete.
examples: The senator gave *full-blooded* support to the plan.
It was a loud, *full-blooded* rock performance.

senses.gloss: Fully developed, with all the features of something.
examples: The argument turned into a *full-blown* fight.
Experts fear a *full-blown* recession.
Her cold turned into *full-blown* pneumonia.

senses.gloss: Of wine, coffee or a sound: rich and strong.
examples: Try a *full-bodied* red with the steak.
This coffee is dark and *full-bodied*.
The cello has a warmer, more *full-bodied* sound than the viola.
